summary: Documents the needs of various industries for multi-hop paths with deterministic properties for characterized flows, such as bounded latency. It frames the problem that the Deterministic Networking work addresses. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: Some applications need network packets to arrive within a predictable time and with very little loss. RFC 8557 describes the problems that a deterministic networking solution must address.

why do industrial networks need bounded latency
what is packet replication elimination and ordering
subtitle: The networking problems behind deterministic multi-hop paths

tldr.problem: Industrial, utility, and other systems need characterized traffic flows with bounded latency and very low loss. Ordinary packet networks do not provide those guarantees under arbitrary load.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC frames requirements for DetNet paths, including flow characterization, resource reservation, path setup, and optional packet replication and elimination.
tldr.outcome: RFC 8557 is a problem statement, not a protocol specification. It describes issues for the DetNet work to address.

today: RFC 8557 is an Informational problem statement and the batch metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC refers to a separate DetNet architecture document and does not specify a protocol.

sections.title: Why Deterministic Networking Is Needed
sections.content:
RFC 8578 describes industries with similar needs for latency guarantees and very low packet loss. As these networks grow beyond local links, they need deterministic forwarding across routed Layer 3 networks as well as Layer 2 networks.

Deterministic Networking (DetNet) aims to carry time-sensitive flows alongside ordinary statistically multiplexed traffic. This document states the problem and discusses what the IETF work should address; the architecture is covered in a separate document.
sections.plainLanguage: Industries want to carry time-sensitive traffic over packet networks without losing its timing and reliability. This RFC states the networking problem rather than defining a solution.

sections.title: Application and Network Needs
sections.content:
The use cases call for synchronized network nodes, flows with bounded minimum and maximum latency, and very low packet loss. Some applications also need low jitter, multicast, and flows that can consume a substantial share of available bandwidth.

Networks must schedule, shape, and limit critical packets at each hop, defend against misbehaving nodes, and reserve resources. The RFC identifies resource reservation before transmission as unavoidable: a network cannot promise finite latency and very low loss for unlimited offered traffic.
sections.plainLanguage: Time-sensitive flows need known timing, reserved resources, and protection from competing traffic. The network cannot promise those properties if senders can transmit without limits.

sections.title: Path Scope and Flow Description
sections.content:
A deterministic path may run end to end between application hosts or form a tunnel between an ingress point and an egress router. The RFC says DetNet does not aim to establish such paths across the global Internet, and notes that the limits of a managed domain need clarification.

Deterministic forwarding applies to flows with defined properties such as periodicity and burstiness. Those characteristics, and how the network will shape and forward the flow, need to be specified before the path is established.
sections.plainLanguage: A DetNet path can connect application hosts or connect two points through a tunnel. The flow's traffic pattern must be described before the network can plan its path.

sections.title: Computing Paths and Handling Redundancy
sections.content:
A centralized model using a Path Computation Element (PCE) can optimize paths globally and per flow. The RFC lists needs for reporting topology and device capabilities, requesting and managing path setup, adapting to events such as link loss, and exposing path status to end devices. It says a distributed alternative may be studied, but the initial focus should be centralized path computation.

Some flows may need copies sent over non-congruent paths to improve delivery. The RFC calls for packet formats and protocols to identify, replicate, eliminate, and, where needed, reorder packets, preferably by reusing an existing solution.
sections.plainLanguage: A central path planner can use network-wide information to reserve a route for a flow. For some flows, copies over separate paths can provide another chance for delivery.

sections.title: Security for Time-Sensitive Flows
sections.content:
For deterministic networks, delivery time can be as important as packet contents. A man-in-the-middle attacker could add or adjust delay and disrupt a real-time application without breaking encryption.

DetNet virtualizes networks that may previously have relied on physical isolation. Security must protect signaling, authenticate and authorize controlling nodes, identify and shape flows, and isolate each flow from leaks or interference caused by shared resources.
sections.plainLanguage: A packet may be harmful if it arrives too late, even when its contents are unchanged. Security must protect timing and isolate reserved flows as well as protect their data.
